narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your class ranking at the end of your third year. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) was a significant red flag; most students who are accepted sit around the middle of their class (average around 5.8). This low ranking strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0 was the second most important factor. Although this pulled the prediction slightly in a more positive direction, it was still below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore could not offset the negative signal from your class rank.

Your LSAT score of 30 was the third most influential piece of information. Like your GPA, it also nudged the prediction mildly toward passing, but it fell well short of the 37.2 average among accepted applicants and was not strong enough to change the overall outlook.

In short, your low class standing in year three outweighed the modest positive effects of your GPA and LSAT, leading the model to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years, retake the LSAT if possible, and consider additional bar-preparation resources before reapplying. Improving any one of these areas substantially could shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
